chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Abi Umayr from Aban ibn Uthman from some of our companions from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

Regarding a man who advances dirhams for food until a due date, and when the food becomes due he says: 'I do not have food, but look at its value and take its price from me.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no harm in that.'

Sahl ibn Ziyad from Mu'awiya ibn Hakim from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhl said: I wrote to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him): 'A man advances me food, and when the time comes and I do not have food, should I give him dirhams equal to its value?' He said: 'Yes.'

As for the one narrated by Muhammad ibn Yahya from Bunan ibn Muhammad from Musa ibn al-Qasim from Ali ibn Ja'far who said: I asked him about a man who has dates, or barley, or wheat owed to him by another, should he take dirhams equal to their value? He said: 'If he values them in dirhams, it is invalid, because the principal by which he buys is dirhams, so dirhams are not suitable for dirhams.'
And I asked him about a man who gave his servant ten dirhams on condition that the servant pays back ten dirhams every month, is that permissible? He said: 'There is no harm in it.'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: The ruling I give is what this last report entails: that if what was advanced was dirhams, it is not permissible for him to sell it back to him with dirhams, because he would be selling dirhams for dirhams, and there might be an increase or decrease, and that is usury.

And there is no contradiction between this report and the first two, because the first report is disconnected (mursal) and not fully chained, and if it were chained, his saying 'Look at its value and take its price from me' could mean he meant: 'Look at its value at the price you took from me,' because we have clarified that it is permissible for him to take the value with the principal amount without increase or decrease.

And the second report is similar, and neither of the two reports states that he gives him the value at the current price, and if what we mentioned is possible, then there is no contradiction between them in any case.

Moreover, the two reports allow for another meaning: that it was permissible for him to take dirhams equal to the value if he had given him something other than dirhams at the time of the advance, and that would not lead to usury due to the difference in kind, and specifically the first report, because it does not go beyond stating that it is permissible for him to take the price, and it does not state that he takes the price from the same kind as what he gave or from another kind.
ai.seo_question: Can a debtor pay back a food loan with cash instead of food?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi synthesizes these narrations to resolve the apparent contradiction between permissibility and prohibition by distinguishing between *sarf* (currency exchange) and *bay'* (sale); if the original loan was in food, paying with dirhams is permissible as a sale of a different genus, but if the loan was in dirhams, paying with dirhams risks *riba* due to potential inequality in value. This reflects the Shia juristic principle that *riba* in currency exchanges strictly requires equality in both quantity and quality, whereas food-for-money transactions allow for market value variations. The scholar emphasizes that the permissibility hinges on whether the transaction is viewed as settling a debt of a specific commodity or exchanging like-for-like currency.
